paragraphs: Domain adaptation concerns learning when the distribution supplying training examples differs from the distribution encountered at test time. This paper develops a PAC-Bayesian analysis of that problem, connecting guarantees about prediction to a framework that reasons about distributions over classifiers. The authors present this as the first PAC-Bayesian treatment of domain adaptation.

The central construction measures differences between domains through average classifier disagreement. Rather than describing distribution differences independently of prediction, it uses how classifiers disagree to define a new pseudodistance. The authors then use this quantity to bound the performance of a stochastic Gibbs classifier. A useful feature of the bound is that it can be optimized directly for any hypothesis space.

The paper specializes the analysis to linear classifiers and derives a learning algorithm from it. Experiments on a synthetic problem and a sentiment annotation task produce results the authors describe as interesting. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical framework and a concrete algorithm, opening a route for applying further PAC-Bayesian tools to adaptation.
icml-2013-a-pac-bayesian-approach-for-do.tldr: A disagreement-based PAC-Bayesian bound provides an optimizable framework for domain adaptation and yields a concrete algorithm for linear classifiers.

paragraphs: Bayesian reinforcement learning must connect observations of an environment with uncertainty about how that environment works. This can be difficult when a detailed simulator exists but writing down a probabilistic model of the underlying process is too complex. The paper proposes ABC-RL, a general framework that uses Approximate Bayesian Computation to support learning in this situation.

Its key requirement is a prior distribution over a class of simulators. This lets the framework approach inference without requiring an explicitly formulated likelihood for the process. The authors describe ABC-RL as allowing any Bayesian reinforcement learning technique to be used in this setting. Simulation consequently supports both planning what to do and inference about the environment.

The paper supplies an experimental comparison with LSPI to demonstrate the approach's potential. It also introduces a theorem establishing the soundness of ABC. These contributions address different questions: the experiments illustrate practical promise, while the theorem supplies theoretical support for the inference approach. The stated practical opportunity is to make detailed simulation models usable within Bayesian reinforcement learning.
icml-2013-abc-reinforcement-learning-913.tldr: ABC-RL enables likelihood-free Bayesian reinforcement learning using a prior over simulators, with theoretical support and an experimental demonstration.

paragraphs: Cross-validation, online training, and parallel training organize learning in different ways, but this paper develops algorithms for all three through abstract algebra. The central idea is to identify algebraic structure in a classifier's training process. Once an appropriate structure is established, the generic algorithms can be applied to that classification model.

For some models, this structure is straightforward to supply. The authors explicitly construct it for Bayesian classifiers and for HomStumps, a new variation of decision stumps. Other classifiers do not expose an obvious structure. To address that obstacle, the paper introduces the Free HomTrainer, a construction that can provide a generic algebraic structure to any classifier.

The authors apply the Free HomTrainer to bagging and boosting. This leads to new online and parallel algorithms, together with what they describe as the first fast cross-validation schemes for these classifiers. The broader contribution is a reusable route from mathematical structure to training algorithms. Applying that route still requires establishing the relevant structure, either directly or through the generic construction.
icml-2013-algebraic-classifiers-a-generi.tldr: Algebraic structure provides a common route to fast cross-validation, online learning, and parallel training, including new methods for bagging and boosting.

paragraphs: Class labels can carry relationships that help a recognition system distinguish objects. Existing approaches considered here mainly preserve semantic distances between pairs of classes. This paper instead models analogies: relationships in which one class relates to another in the same way that a second pair does. That lets semantic information connect several class relationships at once.

The method translates these analogies into geometric constraints called analogical parallelograms. These constraints enter a convex regularizer for a label embedding learned to support discrimination between classes. The geometry therefore encourages the learned representation to preserve relationships between pairs, extending the influence of semantic knowledge beyond individual pairwise distances.

The authors also explain how to discover analogies from class descriptions expressed through attributes and prioritize those likely to reduce confusion between classes. On two visual recognition datasets, their Analogy-preserving Semantic Embedding improves both recognition accuracy and analogy completion over existing approaches. Those results support the usefulness of preserving relational structure for classification as well as for recovering analogies.
icml-2013-analogy-preserving-semantic-em.tldr: Preserving analogies between class relationships improves visual recognition and analogy completion on two datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision-making in adversarial deterministic Markov decision processes with bandit feedback. The learner must choose actions while receiving limited feedback about their consequences. Performance is measured through regret relative to the best fixed policy chosen in hindsight, so the comparison asks how much is lost by learning during interaction rather than knowing that policy beforehand.

The proposed algorithm improves the regret bound from the previous O(T^3/4) rate to O(T^2/3), where T represents the interaction horizon. The smaller exponent means the stated cumulative regret guarantee grows more slowly with the horizon. The comparator remains a fixed policy in hindsight; the result does not claim comparison with an unrestricted sequence of changing policies.

A separate contribution concerns the arrangement of states and transitions. Earlier approaches required additional restrictions on the process's graph topology. The new algorithm and analysis accommodate any feasible topology within the adversarial deterministic setting. Thus the paper improves both the regret rate and the range of graph structures covered by the guarantee.
icml-2013-better-rates-for-any-adversari.tldr: A new algorithm improves regret to O(T^2/3) for adversarial deterministic MDPs with bandit feedback while accommodating any feasible graph topology.

paragraphs: Structured prediction jointly predicts outputs that depend on one another. A training example can therefore contain substantial internal structure, even when the number of examples is small. Existing distribution-free generalization bounds fail to guarantee learning in this setting, despite empirical evidence that such models can perform well across several application areas.

The paper identifies sufficient conditions for generalization from even one structured example. These combine weak dependence, control of hypothesis complexity, and a new measure called collective stability. The analysis does not require an explicit generative model of the data. Its guarantee is conditional on these properties, rather than a claim that any single large example necessarily supports reliable learning.

The authors show that a broad class of models satisfies the complexity and stability conditions, including marginal inference in templated graphical models. They obtain uniform convergence rates that can improve substantially on previous bounds. The improvement is especially relevant when each example is sufficiently large while the number of training examples stays fixed, potentially at one.
icml-2013-collective-stability-in-struct.tldr: Weak dependence, controlled complexity, and collective stability provide sufficient conditions for generalization from even one large structured example.

paragraphs: Linear regression can require a choice between statistical accuracy and computational cost. This paper constructs a family of estimators that makes that choice adjustable and mathematically explicit. The estimators combine hard thresholding of sample covariance entries with ridge regularization, providing two parameters through which the statistical and computational behavior can be studied.

Thresholding introduces sparsity into the covariance representation, while regularization also affects the resulting estimation problem. The authors analyze predictive risk as a function of both choices. With appropriate parameters, computing the estimator reduces to solving a sparse, diagonally dominant linear system. That structure permits a solver whose running time is near-linear.

The main result connects computationally useful structure with its consequences for prediction. The analysis explains how risk changes with sparsity and regularization, establishing a smooth tradeoff rather than presenting speed and accuracy as unrelated outcomes. Simulations support the theoretical findings. The near-linear computational claim depends on choosing parameters that produce the specified linear-system structure.
icml-2013-computation-risk-tradeoffs-for.tldr: Thresholding covariance entries and adding ridge regularization yields an explicit tradeoff between predictive risk and computation, with near-linear solving under suitable choices.

paragraphs: A consistent classification loss connects minimizing expected loss with achieving accuracy close to the Bayes optimum. This paper shows why that desirable property can be insufficient for comparing losses when the learner uses a restricted class of scoring functions. Its focus is multiclass prediction with linear scoring functions and data that are linearly separable.

The authors construct a sequence of data sources where optimizing the Crammer–Singer loss produces expected error tending to zero. On the same sequence, optimizing a generalized LogitBoost loss leaves error bounded below by a positive constant. This is striking because the former loss is known to lack ordinary consistency, while the latter possesses it. Both theoretical and experimental results exhibit the difference.

The explanation is realizable consistency relative to the restricted scoring class. The paper proves that Crammer–Singer has this property for linear scoring functions, whereas generalized LogitBoost does not. The LogitBoost result follows from a broader theorem covering other multiclass losses. The lesson concerns matching guarantees to the scoring class, rather than universally ranking these losses.
icml-2013-consistency-versus-realizable-.tldr: For restricted linear scoring functions, realizable consistency can explain performance differences that ordinary multiclass loss consistency does not.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation requires understanding how training and test distributions differ. This paper separates three possibilities using features X and targets Y. Target shift changes the distribution of Y while preserving the distribution of X given Y. Conditional shift preserves the target distribution but changes the conditional distribution under constraints. Generalized target shift permits both kinds of change, again constraining the conditional change.

The authors use causal interpretations and background knowledge to determine which situation fits a problem. They then adapt learning through importance reweighting or transformations of the samples. The weights or transformations are estimated by making the adjusted training data reproduce the feature distribution observed in the test domain.

Kernel embeddings represent both conditional and marginal distributions, allowing the methods to avoid explicit distribution estimation. This makes the proposed approaches applicable to high-dimensional problems. Evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. Its central contribution is to connect different assumptions about distribution change with corresponding ways to adjust training data.
icml-2013-domain-adaptation-under-target.tldr: A domain adaptation framework uses shift-specific assumptions, reweighting or sample transformations, and kernel embeddings to match training data to the test domain.

paragraphs: Interpretable classifiers can express decisions through logical rules, but finding the correct rules is computationally difficult. This paper connects rule learning to Boolean compressed sensing. It treats learning a single conjunctive clause, which combines conditions with AND, or a single disjunctive clause, which combines them with OR, as a Boolean group testing problem.

The authors introduce a linear programming relaxation for solving these problems. They also derive conditions for exact recovery that parallel sparse-signal recovery results in compressed sensing. The general rule recovery problem remains NP-hard. Exact recovery is guaranteed under certain conditions on the Boolean sensing matrix, making the contribution a conditional theoretical result rather than a general solution to the hard problem.

To build complete classifiers, the method combines learned clauses into rule sets using set covering and boosting. The resulting approach achieves competitive classification accuracy. Its significance is the combination of interpretable rule construction with exact recovery theory, extending a field where much previous work relied on heuristic solutions.
icml-2013-exact-rule-learning-via-boolea.tldr: Boolean compressed sensing yields interpretable rule learners with conditional exact-recovery guarantees and competitive classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Learning related tasks together can improve performance, but sharing information with unrelated tasks can cause serious degradation. This paper proposes a multitask framework that learns how tasks are related instead of committing to uniform sharing. It groups tasks in a low-dimensional subspace and allows the groups themselves to share subspace bases.

That construction supports several degrees of relatedness. Unrelated groups can avoid sharing, while related groups can share some or all of their bases. The number of groups and the subspace dimensionality are inferred from data. To provide this flexibility, the authors extend a hierarchical beta process prior using a Dirichlet process, permitting potentially infinitely many child beta processes.

The model is applied to both regression and classification across multiple tasks. Experiments on several synthetic and real-world datasets report better performance than other recent state-of-the-art multitask methods. The stated advantage is a flexible representation of task relationships: the model can choose both how much structure to use and where sharing should occur.
icml-2013-factorial-multi-task-learning-.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric multitask model learns task groups, subspace size, and degrees of sharing, outperforming comparison methods in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Some learning features come from human judgments rather than precise measurements. Such judgments can be subjective, noisy, or difficult to define consistently. The paper starts from the possibility that asking several people to judge the same feature on the same object can be useful. This makes repeated measurement a meaningful part of feature selection.

The proposed feature multi-selection algorithms make two connected decisions: which features to obtain and how many judgments to collect for each. The authors describe these algorithms as theoretically motivated. Their formulation extends the usual choice of a feature subset by allowing different amounts of repetition across features, so selecting a feature does not settle how it should be measured.

The approach is demonstrated with linear regression on a crowdsourced task predicting height and weight from photographs. The candidate features include gender judgments, estimated weight, and culturally subjective attractiveness judgments. The reported results demonstrate the approach's effectiveness in that task. They support considering repeated judgments during selection without establishing that every subjective feature benefits equally from repetition.
icml-2013-feature-multi-selection-among-.tldr: Feature multi-selection chooses both which subjective features to collect and how many judgments to obtain for each.

paragraphs: Sequential classification must account for both complex relationships within observations and changes over time. This paper combines large-margin kernel classifiers with Bayesian nonparametric modeling to address both. Its model contains a theoretically infinite collection of interdependent classifier components, intended to capture local nonlinear structure in complex data.

A Markov-switching construction connects the components, allowing the active classification behavior to follow temporal dynamics. Stick-breaking priors govern this switching mechanism and let Bayesian inference determine how many components to use from the data. The infinite formulation therefore supplies flexibility in model size, while component selection is driven by the observations.

Training uses maximum entropy discrimination, a framework that combines the large-margin principle with Bayesian posterior inference. The authors describe the training as efficient and evaluate the method on several real-world datasets against state-of-the-art alternatives. The paper's stated contribution is this integrated model of nonlinear classification, temporal switching, and adaptable component count. The abstract reports the evaluation but does not specify a comparative performance outcome.
icml-2013-infinite-markov-switching-maxi.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric Markov-switching model combines large-margin classifiers with temporal dynamics and a data-driven number of components.

paragraphs: Standard LDA represents documents through collections of discrete words. This paper extends it to data more naturally described by continuous descriptors. A finite dictionary supplies generative models for those descriptors, and each descriptor can be assigned softly to several dictionary words. This preserves ambiguity that a single hard assignment would discard.

The authors derive variational inference and parameter estimation procedures resembling those for ordinary LDA. Two changes are central. Ordinary word counts become pseudo-counts obtained by summing assignment responsibilities. Parameter estimation also accounts for covariance between those pseudo-counts, because soft assignment creates dependencies between words. The extension therefore changes both the representation and the way its uncertainty enters estimation.

The application is novelty detection in video, where events with low posterior probability are identified as unusual. Dynamic texture models describe events and provide a dictionary of generative words. On a benchmark dataset, the soft-assignment model substantially improves novel-event detection over hard-assignment LDA and achieves results reported as state of the art.
icml-2013-lda-topic-model-with-soft-assi.tldr: Extending LDA with soft descriptor-to-word assignments and dependent pseudo-counts substantially improves video novelty detection on a benchmark.

paragraphs: Understanding an activity involves recognizing what happened and anticipating what will happen next and how. This paper addresses both tasks using RGB-D video. It begins with a conditional random field that models spatial and temporal relationships between human poses and objects, including the affordances involved in their interaction.

An activity contains smaller subactivities, but their temporal boundaries can be ambiguous. Different segmentations imply different graph structures, for both past observations and possible futures. The method explicitly reasons over several structures. It first approximates the graph using additive features, enabling efficient dynamic programming, and then modifies the resulting proposal to generate additional likely structures.

Considering alternative structures allows ambiguity in activity decomposition to enter the inference process. The authors report significant improvements over the state of the art for both detecting past activities and anticipating future ones. These results come from a dataset of 120 activity videos collected from four subjects. The finding supports the proposed structural reasoning approach within that evaluated setting.
icml-2013-learning-spatio-temporal-struc.tldr: Reasoning over alternative activity graph structures improves recognition and anticipation in an RGB-D dataset of 120 videos from four subjects.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning builds a codebook that provides a representation for later learning tasks. The paper positions this as an important abstraction step: what the codebook captures affects the information available to a classifier. Existing approaches discussed by the authors include unsupervised generative methods and supervised discriminative methods. They propose a weakly supervised alternative based on multiple-instance learning.

Each code is represented by a classifier, such as a linear support vector machine. This representation naturally supports metric fusion across multiple feature channels. The learning formulation jointly learns mixtures of codes by maximizing classification margins within the multiple-instance framework. Codebook construction is therefore directly connected to a discriminative objective.

The learned codebooks are evaluated on image classification benchmarks, where the authors report state-of-the-art results together with compact and effective representations. These findings indicate that the proposed learning strategy can produce useful codebooks without requiring the representation to follow either of the two existing approaches alone. The main contribution is the multiple-instance, margin-based formulation for learning the codes jointly.
icml-2013-max-margin-multiple-instance-d.tldr: A multiple-instance, maximum-margin approach learns compact classifier-based codebooks that achieve state-of-the-art results on image classification benchmarks.

paragraphs: Information, ideas, behaviors, and diseases can spread through networks whose connections are not directly observed. This paper uses survival theory to infer such networks from propagation data. It develops additive and multiplicative risk models, describing how activity at one node relates to the risk that another node becomes active.

The additive formulation provides a common model containing several existing network inference approaches as special cases. The multiplicative formulation adds the ability to represent influences that either increase or decrease another node's activation risk. This extends the range of interactions beyond the positive risk increments considered by previous approaches. Both formulations yield inference problems whose convexity can be exploited for efficient solution.

The authors evaluate their inference algorithms on large synthetic and real cascade datasets. They also show that the models can predict cascade length and duration in real data. These results connect network reconstruction with observable propagation behavior. The contribution combines a unifying model family, a way to represent opposing influences, and computationally tractable inference.
icml-2013-modeling-information-propagati.tldr: Survival-based risk models enable efficient network inference, including influences that suppress activation, and predict cascade length and duration in real data.

paragraphs: Autoencoders learn representations, but they can also be used to score how well data fit what they represent. Existing scoring approaches often rely on training criteria that connect an autoencoder to a probabilistic model, such as a restricted Boltzmann machine. This paper develops a different foundation for obtaining meaningful, unnormalized scores.

The authors interpret an autoencoder as a dynamical system. They investigate when running that system can be understood as gradient descent on an energy function. Under the relevant conditions, integration provides a score derived from that energy interpretation. This connects the autoencoder's behavior to scoring independently of its training procedure and without requiring a separate probabilistic model.

The conditional energy interpretation is central: the paper examines when it applies, rather than asserting that every autoencoder automatically has the needed structure. It also shows how several unnormalized scores can be combined into a generative classifier. The contribution thus extends from interpreting an individual autoencoder to using multiple scores together for classification.
icml-2013-on-autoencoder-scoring-a94e8e3.tldr: Viewing autoencoders as dynamical systems yields meaningful scores under suitable energy-function conditions and supports combining scores into a generative classifier.

paragraphs: A hidden Markov model describes observations through hidden states and the probabilities of moving between them. This paper studies models whose observations belong to a parametric distribution family. Its main strategy separates learning what each hidden state emits from learning how the hidden state changes over time, producing a two-stage estimation procedure.

First, the method fits a mixture model to the stationary distribution of the observations. This estimates the output-distribution parameters. Given those estimates, the second stage learns hidden-state transition probabilities through a convex quadratic program that the authors describe as easy to solve. Separating the stages gives the transition estimation problem a particularly tractable form.

The paper analyzes errors in the estimated transition probabilities, including the consequences of imperfect output estimates. It shows robustness to small perturbations in the mixture parameters. That result matters because the second stage necessarily depends on quantities estimated in the first. Encouraging empirical results support the analysis, complementing the theoretical account of how estimation errors carry through the procedure.
icml-2013-on-learning-parametric-output-.tldr: A two-stage HMM learner estimates output distributions first, then learns transitions through convex optimization with robustness to small first-stage errors.

paragraphs: Many optimization procedures can be understood as repeatedly replacing an objective with a surrogate and minimizing that surrogate. This paper studies that shared pattern through first-order surrogate functions. The aim is to explain several established techniques within one framework while also using the framework to construct additional algorithms for machine learning optimization.

The authors propose several algorithmic variants and provide simple convergence analyses. Their unified viewpoint encompasses accelerated proximal gradient, block coordinate descent, and Frank–Wolfe methods. Bringing these techniques into the same account makes their surrogate-minimization structure explicit, connecting algorithms that are often presented separately through a common way of organizing successive optimization steps.

The paper also introduces a new incremental scheme. In experiments on large-scale optimization problems typical of machine learning, it matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art solvers. That is an empirical finding about the evaluated problems. Together, the conceptual framework and the new scheme show how studying existing optimization methods through surrogates can produce both explanatory and practical contributions.
icml-2013-optimization-with-first-order-.tldr: First-order surrogate functions unify several optimization methods and lead to an incremental scheme that matches or outperforms leading solvers experimentally.

paragraphs: Sparse regression seeks the relatively small set of features that matter for predicting a response. This paper asks whether that support can still be identified when entries of the feature matrix are corrupted arbitrarily, potentially severely or in coordinated ways. The challenge concerns corrupted covariates, extending beyond methods designed only for corrupted responses or stochastic errors.

The authors show that even a natural exponential-time search does not provide the desired protection. Choosing the subset of data and feature columns with the smallest regression error can still fail to recover the support. Their alternative changes a basic calculation used throughout regression: the inner product. A trimmed inner product limits the influence of a controlled number of arbitrarily corrupted points.

The paper applies this replacement to Thresholding Regression, Lasso, and the Dantzig selector, obtaining counterparts with provable robustness. The contribution is a shared modification to familiar algorithms supported by theory. Its robustness concerns controlled corruption levels; it does not assert successful recovery under an unlimited number of adversarial changes.
icml-2013-robust-sparse-regression-under.tldr: Replacing ordinary inner products with trimmed versions yields provably robust sparse-regression methods under controlled amounts of arbitrary covariate corruption.

paragraphs: Random projection changes the representation of data before a classifier is trained. This paper asks how that change affects prediction on unseen examples for a generic linear classifier trained by empirical risk minimization. The authors derive sharp generalization-error bounds without requiring restrictive data properties such as sparsity or separability.

The analysis centers on predicted class labels. For classification, a geometric change matters especially when it moves an example across a decision boundary and changes its assigned label. The authors derive the exact probability of this label-flipping event under Gaussian random projection. That probability gives a precise way to quantify the effect of the projection in their bounds.

The contribution therefore links projection directly to the decision the classifier makes, rather than treating preservation of geometry as the only question. The absence of sparsity and separability assumptions broadens the stated data setting. The result remains specifically an analysis of linear empirical-risk classifiers and Gaussian projection effects; it quantifies generalization error rather than claiming that projection always preserves every label.
icml-2013-sharp-generalization-error-bou.tldr: Exact label-flipping probabilities under Gaussian random projection yield sharp generalization bounds for linear classifiers without sparsity or separability assumptions.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks a principal direction using only a limited number of coordinates. This paper proposes a combinatorial algorithm for a positive semidefinite matrix. It examines a discrete collection of specially chosen vectors within a low-dimensional eigensubspace, using that reduced spectral representation to approach the sparse component problem.

The approximation guarantees depend on the matrix's eigenvalue profile. Faster eigenvalue decay gives better approximation quality. In particular, for power-law eigenvalue decay, the authors obtain a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for any desired accuracy. This connects the strength of the computational guarantee to a stated property of the matrix rather than promising the same behavior for every spectrum.

A feature elimination step also makes it possible to process datasets containing millions of entries within a few minutes. Experiments on artificial and real datasets find nearly optimal solutions while maintaining very sparse vectors. The method matches or outperforms previous algorithms on every tested dataset. Those empirical findings complement the spectrum-dependent approximation theory.
icml-2013-sparse-pca-through-low-rank-ap.tldr: A low-rank combinatorial approach to sparse PCA offers spectrum-dependent approximation guarantees and strong accuracy and scalability in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a model of temporal behavior usually calls for observations collected in sequence. This paper develops hidden Markov model learning methods that also use independent, unordered snapshots. The motivation is practical: snapshots are often easier to obtain than full time series, so a learner that can use both kinds of data has access to additional information.

The static observations are assumed to come from the HMM's stationary distribution. Building on existing spectral algorithms, the proposed methods solve convex optimization problems. The objective combines squared loss on the dynamic observations with a regularization term derived from the static observations. Sequential data and unordered data thus contribute differently to the same learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic data and real human activity data show better prediction than existing spectral algorithms. These results support incorporating the available stationary snapshots alongside temporal observations. The contribution is specifically a way to combine the two data sources in spectral HMM learning, with the static information influencing the fitted model through regularization.
icml-2013-spectral-learning-of-hidden-ma.tldr: Spectral HMM learners improve prediction in reported experiments by combining time-series loss with regularization from independent stationary snapshots.

paragraphs: Coactive learning allows a system to learn from user preferences during ordinary use. A search engine, for example, can receive weak, often implicit feedback instead of fully specified correct answers. This paper shows that existing online algorithms for this setting can become unstable and ineffective when feedback contains substantial bias and noise.

The proposed method explores small perturbations to the objects presented to users, such as rankings. These changes are used to stabilize the learning process. The authors present the resulting algorithm as the first coactive learner able to learn robustly despite biased and noisy feedback. The intervention is therefore part of the interaction itself, connecting presentation choices to the reliability of subsequent learning.

The paper supplies bounds on average regret as theoretical validation. It also evaluates the method on benchmarks and in a live search engine user study, reporting substantial improvements over existing methods. These two forms of evidence support the proposed stabilization strategy: the analysis characterizes learning performance, while the evaluations examine its effectiveness with practical feedback.
icml-2013-stable-coactive-learning-via-p.tldr: Slightly perturbing presented objects stabilizes coactive learning under biased, noisy feedback, with regret bounds and substantial empirical gains.
